'''David Arthur Shirley''' (March 30, 1934 – March 29, 2021) was an American chemist, best known as the fourth director of the [[Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory]] from 1980 to 1989, and for spearheading the funding and creation of the [[Advanced Light Source]].

==Biography==
David Arthur Shirley was born in [[North Conway, New Hampshire]], on March 30, 1934.<ref name="ACAP">{{cite web |url=https://www.aip.org/history/acap/biographies/bio.jsp?shirleyd |title=David Shirley |publisher=Array of Contemporary American Physicists |accessdate=18 April 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160507100102/https://www.aip.org/history/acap/biographies/bio.jsp?shirleyd |archive-date=7 May 2016 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name="Thesis">{{cite web |url=https://search.library.berkeley.edu/permalink/01UCS_BER/1thfj9n/alma991066352239706532 |title=The heat capacities and entropies of iodine and lithium chloride from 15 to 325 degrees Kelvin |first=David Arthur |last=Shirley |publisher=[[University of California, Berkeley]] |date=January 1959 }}</ref> He earned a [[Bachelor of Science]] degree in [[chemistry]] from the [[University of Maine]] in 1955,<ref name="80th Birthday Symposium">{{cite web |url=http://users.physik.fu-berlin.de/~wbrewer/ShirleySymposium-Dateien/Stoehr_Shirley-Laudatio.pdf |title=In Honor of David Shirley, Person, Scientist and Leader: 80th Birthday Symposium |location=Berlin |date=July 4, 2014 |first=Joachim |last=Stöhr |authorlink=Joachim Stöhr |publisher=[[Free University of Berlin]] |accessdate=18 April 2016}}</ref> and then entered the [[University of California, Berkeley]], where he completed his [[PhD]], writing his 1959 doctoral thesis on "The heat capacities and entropies of iodine and lithium chloride from 15 to 325 degrees Kelvin", under the supervision of [[William Giauque]].<ref name="Thesis" />

Shirley married Virginia Schultz in 1956, and they had five children together, David, Diane, Michael, Eric and Gail Shirley. Shirley has a total of eleven grandchildren, Brian, Arthur, Kevin, Colleen, Sarah, Lauren, Catalina, Wendell, Wilbur, Darian and Madelyn.<ref>{{cite web|title=In Memoriam – Virginia Shirley| url=http://www2.lbl.gov/Publications/Currents/Archive/Mar-31-1995.html#RTFToC5|website=lbl.gove|access-date=August 28, 2020}}</ref>

Shirley became a lecturer in chemistry at Berkeley in 1959, an [[assistant professor]] in 1960, an [[associate professor]] in 1964, and a full [[professor]] in 1967. The following year he became chairman of the Chemistry Department.<ref name="80th Birthday Symposium" /> He was a [[National Science Foundation]] fellow at [[Oxford University]] in 1966–67,<ref name="ACAP" /> and was awarded the [[United States Atomic Energy Commission]]'s [[Ernest Orlando Lawrence Award]] in 1972. His early research was into [[low temperature physics]], [[nuclear orientation]], and [[Hyperfine structure|hyperfine interactions]], particularly the [[Mössbauer effect]], and he was a pioneer of [[X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy]].<ref name="80th Birthday Symposium" />

In 1975, Shirley became the Associate Laboratory Director and Head, Materials and Molecular Research Division of the [[Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory]].<ref name="ACAP" /> He was its fourth director, from 1980 to 1989,<ref name="80th Birthday Symposium" /> and was the first chemist to head the laboratory. He took the helm at a time when the laboratory had to deal with deep funding cuts, and spent most of his first two years in the job managing them. Having weathered the crisis, he attempted to prevent its recurrence by broadening the range of research projects, such as research into treatments for [[ocular melanoma]], and development of [[Mina Bissell]]'s [[extracellular matrix]] model of [[breast cancer]]. In 1987, the Lawrence Berkeley Laboratory was chosen to participate in the [[Human Genome Project]].<ref name="An Historical Perspective" />

Another initiative was the Center for Advanced Materials (CAM). In turn, this led to the establishment of the Center for X-Ray Optics (CXRO), the world's first research facility devoted to specialise in the use of [[soft x-ray]]s and [[extreme ultraviolet]] light known as XUV. As it turned out, these are ideal for manipulating the atoms and molecules on materials' surfaces, where most chemical reactions take place. In 1984, Shirley proposed the construction of the [[Advanced Light Source]], a [[synchrotron]] optimized to produce XUV. Not everyone saw the value in it, but the scientific case was sound, and Shirley eventually secured $100 million of funding from the [[United States Secretary of Energy|Secretary of Energy]], [[John S. Herrington]]. It was the first synchrotron to be built at Berkeley in almost thirty years, and was built on the site of [[Ernest Lawrence]]'s 184-inch synchrotron.<ref name="An Historical Perspective">{{cite web |url=http://www2.lbl.gov/Publications/75th/files/04-lab-history-pt-6.html |title=An Historical Perspective on the Lab's Legacy: A Year-Long Series in The View: Part Six |publisher=[[Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory]] |accessdate=18 April 2016}}</ref>

Shirley stepped down as director of the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory on August 31, 1989,<ref name="An Historical Perspective" /> but remained at Berkeley as a professor. In 1992 he accepted a position as senior vice president for research and graduate education at [[Pennsylvania State University]]. He increased the number of minorities in graduate school, and reduced the average time to graduate. Although this was a time when the [[United States Congress]] was cutting Federal funding for research, he positioned the university so as to make the best of available opportunities, and cemented its place as the premier state university in the country for research funding from industry. He retired at the end of 1996, and returned to California with his second wife, Barbara.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.psu.edu/ur/archives/PEOPLE/Shirley.html |title=Shirley To Retire At End Of Year |date=April 24, 1996 |accessdate=18 April 2016}}</ref>
